title: My two properties don't suit me any more. How do I move out now?
excerpt: A buyer with a Rumawip she can't sell until 2026 and a new launch still under construction has outgrown both. Sean suggests renting a home for now and treating both units as investments.

question.asker: From YY, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: In 2016 YY bought a 1,035 sq ft Rumawip for RM300,000 near her parents, with a 10-year moratorium on selling until 2026; its rent falls about RM300 short of the instalment. In 2021 she bought a RM500,000, 1,000 sq ft new launch on Old Klang Road for her family, due in 2025. Her income has since risen, she has a young child, still lives with her parents and now wants a bigger home with better facilities.
question.text: What should she do, given she wants to move out as soon as possible and can't sell either property yet?

answer.quote: Renting where I stay, buying where I invest.
answer.summary: Rent a bigger home now and learn what she really needs, sell the Rumawip once the moratorium ends, and rent out the Old Klang Road unit when it is handed over. Buy the dream home later, when her income, family and needs have settled.

reasons.title: Life changes faster than buildings
reasons.body: High-rise projects take 48 to 60 months to complete, and in that time income, marriage and children can change what you need. Sean bought a home for each stage of life until he decided to rent instead.

reasons.title: Renting teaches you what you want
reasons.body: Living in a larger rented unit for about two years shows what size kitchen, how many bedrooms and which facilities you really use, before you commit to a dream home.

reasons.title: Waiting ties up a loan slot
reasons.body: An under-construction purchase uses one of your two 90% loan slots for years, so a promotion or pay rise can't be put to work in another property until it completes.

reasons.title: You can still buy the project later
reasons.body: If you liked a project at launch you can buy it as a subsale after completion. Within about six months of handover many owners want to sell, which is when you can negotiate a better price.

actions: Rent a larger, fully furnished unit on a two-year lease and move out of your parents' home.
Look into why a Rumawip near an MRT station still can't cover its instalment, and furnish it to push the rent up.
When the moratorium ends, sell the Rumawip to free up your loan slot and cash.
Furnish and rent out the new unit when you get the keys rather than selling it straight away.
Keep viewing properties, around 20, before choosing a home to buy for the long term.
caveat: Sean suggests refinancing through a non-bank lender, such as an insurer, might free another loan slot later, but says he hasn't seen a Rumawip refinanced and the equity may not yet be enough. Telling your parents you are moving out is often harder than the property side.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #244, sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean says he is part of. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in March 2024; Rumawip moratorium rules vary, so check yours.
